# Method for Servicing a Top Drive Device in a Wellbore Drilling Installation

## Overview of the Drilling Installation

The present method concerns the servicing of a top drive device within a wellbore drilling installation. Such an installation comprises several key structural components, including a drilling tower and a drill floor that defines a well center. During drilling operations, drilling tubulars pass along a firing line, which represents the vertical path along which the tubulars are handled and lowered into or raised out of the wellbore.

## System Configuration

The top drive device is supported by a trolley that is guided along a vertical rail, allowing the top drive to travel up and down the drilling tower in a controlled manner. In addition to this arrangement, the installation includes a motion arm assembly featuring an extensible and retractable arm. This motion arm assembly is guided along a separate vertical rail, providing it with independent vertical movement relative to the trolley supporting the top drive device.

## Functional Capabilities of the Motion Arm

The motion arm is designed with an operative reach that encompasses the firing line. This capability enables the arm to handle and position various well center tools as required during operations. For example, the motion arm can support tools such as an iron roughneck tool or a tubular gripper member, bringing these implements into their working positions along the firing line. This flexibility allows the motion arm assembly to serve multiple functions within the drilling installation beyond a single dedicated task.

## Procedure for Removing a Top Drive Motor

When servicing requires the removal of a top drive motor, the method proceeds as follows. First, the motion arm assembly and/or the trolley are positioned relative to one another so that the top drive motor falls within the operative reach of the motion arm. This positioning ensures that the arm can extend to reach and establish a connection with the motor.

Once the motion arm has connected to the top drive motor, the motor is disconnected from the remainder of the top drive device. Notably, the rest of the top drive device remains attached to the trolley throughout this process, ensuring that only the motor is separated for servicing. With the motor disconnected, the motion arm then supports the top drive motor and is able to lift or lower it as needed, facilitating safe and controlled handling during the servicing operation.

# A Method for Servicing a Top Drive Device on a Wellbore Drilling Installation

## Background and Field

The present method relates to the servicing and maintenance of top drive devices used on wellbore drilling installations. Top drive systems represent a critical component of modern drilling operations, providing the rotational power and torque necessary to advance the drill string into the wellbore. Because these systems operate under substantial mechanical loads and are subject to continuous wear, periodic servicing of the top drive motor is essential to maintaining operational reliability and minimizing costly downtime.

Conventional approaches to servicing a top drive motor typically require either the complete removal of the entire top drive device from the trolley or the deployment of dedicated lifting and handling equipment that is not otherwise used during normal drilling operations. Such approaches are time-consuming, require significant deck space and crane availability, and increase the risk associated with lifting heavy components in the working area of the derrick.

## Summary of the Method

The method described herein addresses these shortcomings by repurposing existing installation equipment—specifically, a motion arm assembly—to service the top drive motor. Under normal operating conditions, this motion arm assembly is used to position well center tools, such as an iron roughneck or a tubular gripper, along the firing line of the drilling installation. Rather than requiring a separate, dedicated maintenance system, the present method leverages this already-present equipment to access and support the top drive motor.

## Detailed Description

The motion arm assembly comprises a vertically guided, extensible arm. During normal drilling operations, the arm extends and retracts to move well center tools into and out of the firing line, enabling operations such as making up and breaking out tubular connections. The vertical guidance of the arm allows controlled movement along the axis of the derrick, while its extensible nature permits the arm to reach into the working area with precision.

When servicing of the top drive motor is required, the motion arm assembly is redirected from its conventional tool-positioning function to a servicing function. The extensible arm is brought into position to access and support the top drive motor. Once the arm has engaged and secured the motor, the vertical guidance system enables the controlled lifting or lowering of the motor along the firing line.

A key advantage of this approach is that the top drive motor may be removed, lifted, or lowered while the remainder of the top drive device remains attached to the trolley. In other words, it is not necessary to disassemble or detach the entire top drive assembly from its supporting structure in order to service the motor. This significantly reduces the scope of work required to gain access to the motor and eliminates the need to handle the complete top drive device as a single heavy unit.

## Advantages

By repurposing the motion arm assembly for servicing tasks, the method streamlines maintenance operations in several respects:

- **Reduced equipment requirements:** Because the motion arm assembly is already installed and used for well center tool positioning, no additional dedicated lifting or handling apparatus is required to service the top drive motor.

- **Reduced downtime:** Servicing the motor without removing the entire top drive device from the trolley shortens the maintenance sequence and returns the installation to operational readiness more quickly.

- **Improved safety:** Handling the top drive motor as an isolated component, using a vertically guided and controlled arm, reduces the risks associated with lifting the complete top drive assembly.

- **Efficient use of installation resources:** The dual-purpose use of the motion arm assembly—for both operational tool positioning and maintenance support—maximizes the utility of existing installation equipment.

In summary, the method provides an efficient and cost-effective means of servicing a top drive motor by utilizing a vertically guided, extensible motion arm assembly that is normally employed for positioning well center tools along the firing line, thereby enabling the removal, lifting, or lowering of the motor while the balance of the top drive device remains supported on the trolley.

# Abstract

A method for servicing a top drive on a drilling rig is disclosed, wherein a motion arm assembly facilitates the removal and replacement of a top drive motor. The method includes positioning the motion arm assembly proximate to the top drive, the motion arm assembly comprising an articulating arm mounted to a support structure and configured to engage the top drive motor. The articulating arm is manipulated to align a coupling mechanism with the top drive motor, and the coupling mechanism is secured to the motor. The method further includes decoupling the top drive motor from the top drive assembly and actuating the motion arm assembly to translate the motor along at least one axis of movement, thereby extracting the motor from an operative position. The motion arm assembly supports the weight of the top drive motor during removal, reducing manual handling and mitigating safety hazards associated with elevated servicing operations. A replacement or serviced motor may be reinstalled by reversing the described steps. The method enables efficient maintenance of the top drive at an elevated position on the drilling rig without requiring complete disassembly of the top drive system, thereby reducing rig downtime and improving operational safety.

# Technical Procedure: Top Drive Motor Removal with Trolley-Mounted Assembly Retention

## 1. Purpose and Scope

This procedure describes the steps required to remove an electric or hydraulic drive motor from a top drive system while maintaining the main body, gearbox, and associated components in their mounted position on the mast-guided trolley (guide dolly). This approach reduces rig downtime by avoiding a full top drive removal.

## 2. Safety Prerequisites

**Before beginning work, confirm the following:**

- Drilling operations are suspended and the wellbore is secured.
- Top drive is positioned at a safe, accessible working height (typically at or near the drill floor, or at a designated maintenance platform).
- The main hoisting system is locked out and the traveling block/becket is secured.
- Electrical isolation (LOTO — Lockout/Tagout) is applied to all motor power circuits; verify zero energy at the motor terminals.
- Hydraulic circuits (if applicable) are depressurized and isolated; verify zero residual pressure at gauges.
- Torque wrench system and pipe handler are de-energized.
- Cooling water/lubrication supply lines are isolated and drained as required.
- A pre-lift risk assessment (JSA/JHA) and permit-to-work are completed and signed off.

## 3. Required Equipment

- Rated overhead lifting device or maintenance hoist (verify SWL against motor weight from OEM data plate)
- Certified slings, shackles, and lifting eyes matched to motor lifting points
- Motor support fixture or removal skid (OEM-specified where available)
- Torque tools and calibrated wrenches
- Guide/alignment pins
- Drip trays and containment for residual fluids
- Manufacturer's service manual and torque specification sheets

## 4. Removal Sequence

### 4.1 Preparation

1. Position and secure the top drive so the trolley is locked against the mast guide rails, preventing vertical or lateral movement.
2. Install any OEM-specified mechanical locking devices to fix the trolley/frame in place independent of the drawworks.
3. Clean the motor-to-gearbox interface area to prevent debris ingress during disassembly.

### 4.2 Disconnection of Services

4. Disconnect and label all electrical power and control cabling at the motor junction box. Cap or protect exposed connectors.
5. Disconnect cooling and lubrication lines; cap open ports and place containment beneath.
6. Disconnect any instrumentation (RTDs, encoders, speed sensors, vibration probes) and protect the leads.

### 4.3 Load Support

7. Attach the maintenance hoist or lifting device to the motor's designated lifting lugs.
8. Take up sling tension until the motor weight is fully supported, but before removing fasteners. Confirm the lifting arrangement is vertical and centered over the motor's center of gravity.

### 4.4 Mechanical Separation

9. Remove the coupling guard between the motor output shaft and the gearbox input.
10. Disengage the drive coupling per OEM instructions (e.g., remove coupling bolts or retract the spline/quill connection). Retain coupling hardware.
11. Install guide/alignment pins into two opposing bolt holes on the motor mounting flange to control the motor during withdrawal.
12. Progressively loosen and remove the motor-to-adapter (or motor-to-gearbox) mounting bolts in a cross pattern to relieve load evenly. Retain all fasteners and note their locations.

### 4.5 Withdrawal

13. With all fasteners removed and the motor fully supported, carefully withdraw the motor axially along the guide pins to disengage the pilot register and coupling.
14. Once clear of the pilot fit, lift and translate the motor away from the top drive assembly, maintaining clearance from surrounding structure, hoses, and cabling.
15. Lower the motor onto the prepared support fixture or skid and secure it for transport to the maintenance area.

## 5. Post-Removal Actions

- Protect the exposed gearbox input shaft, coupling, and mating flange with covers to prevent contamination.
- Inspect the coupling, pilot register, and mounting face for wear or damage; document findings.
- Cap all open fluid ports and electrical connectors on the retained top drive assembly.
- Update maintenance records with motor serial number, running hours, and reason for removal.

## 6. Reference Notes

- Always defer to the top drive manufacturer's service manual for model-specific torque values, coupling type, lifting-point locations, and weights.
- Verify component weights against the equipment data plate before selecting lifting gear.
- Photograph or tag all disconnected connections to aid correct reassembly.

---

*This is a generic technical description. Site-specific procedures, OEM documentation, and applicable regulatory requirements (e.g., API, local drilling regulations) take precedence over this general guidance.*

# Servicing Method Summary

Based on the patent components you've described, here's a summary of the servicing method:

## Key Components

- **Drilling Tower (Mast/Derrick):** The vertical structural framework that supports drilling operations and houses the vertical guidance system.

- **Trolley on Vertical Rail:** A movable carriage that travels up and down along a vertical rail mounted on the tower, enabling repositioning of tools and equipment along the tower's height.

- **Top Drive:** The rotational drive system that turns the drill string and can move vertically along the tower to raise, lower, and rotate pipe.

- **Motion Arm Assembly with Iron Roughneck Tool:** An articulating/extendable arm that carries an iron roughneck—an automated tool used for making up (tightening) and breaking out (loosening) threaded pipe connections.

- **Firing Line:** The central vertical axis (well center) where the drill string is aligned over the wellbore during active drilling operations.

## General Servicing Method

The method typically involves:

1. **Positioning the trolley** along the vertical rail to move the motion arm assembly to the required elevation on the tower.

2. **Extending the motion arm** to move the iron roughneck tool into or out of the firing line as needed.

3. **Engaging the iron roughneck** at pipe connections to make up or break out threaded joints during tripping or drilling operations.

4. **Coordinating with the top drive** so the roughneck and drive work together to manage the drill string.

5. **Retracting the arm** away from the firing line when the operation is complete, clearing the path for continued drilling or top drive movement.

# Extensible/Retractable Motion Arm System for Top Drive Maintenance Support

## System Overview

A top drive motor is one of the heaviest and most critical components on a drilling rig, typically weighing between 20,000-40,000 lbs (9,000-18,000 kg). Supporting and manipulating it during maintenance requires a robust, controlled system. Here's a detailed method for using a rail-mounted extensible arm.

## Core Components

### 1. Vertical Rail System
- **Primary rail structure**: Heavy-duty steel I-beam or box-section rail mounted to the mast/derrick structure
- **Load rating**: Must exceed the top drive weight by a safety factor of at least 4:1
- **Guide surfaces**: Precision-machined tracks with hardened wear surfaces
- **Anchoring**: Bolted and welded connections to structural mast members at multiple points

### 2. Traveling Carriage
- **Roller/bearing assembly**: Cam followers or roller bearings engaging the rail
- **Drive mechanism**: Rack-and-pinion, ball screw, or hydraulic cylinder for vertical positioning
- **Locking system**: Positive mechanical locks at intervals (pin locks or ratchet mechanisms)

### 3. Extensible Motion Arm
- **Telescoping sections**: Nested tubular or box-section members
- **Extension actuator**: Hydraulic cylinder(s) providing controlled horizontal reach
- **End effector**: Cradle, hook, or clamping interface matched to top drive lifting points

## Detailed Operating Method

### Phase 1: Preparation and Safety
1. **Secure the drilling operation** — ensure the top drive is de-energized, hydraulic lines depressurized, and the system locked out/tagged out (LOTO)
2. **Verify rail integrity** — inspect rail welds, bolts, and carriage bearings
3. **Position drill string** appropriately (typically slips set, string hung off)
4. **Confirm load ratings** and check hydraulic/pneumatic system pressures

### Phase 2: Arm Deployment
1. **Position the carriage** vertically to align with the top drive's designed lifting points
2. **Engage carriage locks** to fix vertical position
3. **Extend the motion arm** horizontally toward the top drive using the hydraulic actuator
4. **Control extension rate** via a proportional valve for smooth, precise positioning

### Phase 3: Load Engagement
1. **Align the end effector** with the top drive's lifting lugs, trunnions, or dedicated support points
2. **Engage the connection** — insert locking pins or close hydraulic clamps
3. **Verify positive engagement** through visual inspection and sensor feedback (proximity switches, pin-position indicators)
4. **Take up initial load** gradually while monitoring for proper seating

### Phase 4: Supporting and Lifting
1. **Transfer load** from the traveling block/becket to the arm system by slowly lifting
2. **Monitor load cells** integrated into the arm to confirm weight transfer and avoid overload
3. **Lift or lower** using the carriage vertical drive as needed for access
4. **Extend/retract** horizontally to move the top drive away from the well center for improved maintenance clearance
5. **Lock all axes** once positioned to create a stable work platform

## Critical Engineering Considerations

### Load Management
- **Redundant load sensing**: Multiple load cells with automatic alarms and shutdowns
- **Overload protection**: Pressure relief valves and mechanical stops
- **Center of gravity control**: The arm must account for the top drive's offset CG to prevent tipping moments

### Motion Control
- **Hydraulic counterbalance valves**: Prevent uncontrolled descent if a line fails
- **Pilot-operated check valves**: Hold position under load without drift
- **Redundant locking**: Never rely solely on hydraulic pressure to hold the load

### Structural Stability
- **Moment loads**: Extended arm creates significant bending moments—the carriage and rail must resist these
- **Deflection limits**: Arm deflection under full load must remain within acceptable tolerances
- **Anti-sway measures**: Guides or dampers to control pendulum motion

## Safety Systems

| System | Function |
|--------|----------|
| Emergency stop | Immediate halt of all motion |
| Load monitoring | Real-time weight display with alarms |
| Position sensors | Confirm arm/carriage location |
| Mechanical locks | Positive backup to hydraulic holds |
| Anti-two-block | Prevent carriage from overtraveling |
| Pressure monitoring | Detect hydraulic system faults |

## Advantages of This Method

- **Improved access**: Moves the top drive clear of well center
- **Reduced manual handling**: Minimizes crane dependency and personnel exposure
- **Controlled positioning**: Precise, repeatable movements
- **Safety**: Eliminates workers underneath suspended loads via mechanical locks

## Key Precautions

⚠️ Always maintain redundant support—never rely on a single point of hold  
⚠️ Follow manufacturer load charts and never exceed rated capacity  
⚠️ Account for dynamic loads from rig movement (especially offshore)  
⚠️ Ensure proper training and certification for operators  

---
